entries.title: Woman charged in fatal South Shore shooting
entries.summary: <p>A woman has been charged in a fatal shooting that killed a man last week in South Shore, according to Chicago police.</p><p>Cecelia Morrison Payne, 31, was charged with first-degree murder in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/09/03/37-year-old-man-fatally-shot-in-south-shore-area" target="_blank" >the Sept. 3 shooting</a>, police said.</p><p>A man, 37, was in front of a business in the 7300 block of South Stony Island Avenue when Payne allegedly fatally shot him in the chest, police said.</p><p>Payne is due in court Monday, police said.</p>

entries.title: White Sox maximizing their strength, ranking fifth in percentage of runs via home run
entries.summary: <p>When Munetaka Murakami homered Saturday, the White Sox had themselves the franchise’s first trio of players with at least 30 home runs in a season since 2008 and their fourth trio or foursome in team history.</p><p>Murakami joined Miguel Vargas, who was the first to 30, and Colson Montgomery. After Randal Grichuk and Kyle Teel homered in a 10-1 victory Sunday night against the Twins, the Sox rank fifth in the majors with 188 home runs.</p><p>The Sox have ridden the long ball to first place in the American League Central with 19 games left in the regular season. In fact, of the six division leaders, the Sox are the only team with more than one player with at least 30 homers.</p><p>Considering the Sox are so dependent on home runs, it’s fair to wonder if they’re getting the most out of them. Are they maximizing their biggest strength?</p><p>“The question is are you maximizing the personnel that you have on the field,” Sox hitting coach Derek Shomon told the Sun-Times. “This group is largely a decisions and a damage group. There is some swing and miss.</p><p>“That’s what you try to attack more than anything, but also understanding it may only get marginally better, so you have to lean into the things that you do well. This is an offense that does not chase, that will take their walks and can leave the yard at any time.”</p><p>Shomon’s comment about the Sox being “a decisions and a damage group” comes from their hitting tenets: swing decisions, making contact and doing damage. The contact part has been a problem. The Sox rank sixth in the majors in strikeouts with 1,301. No other division leader is in the top 10.</p><p>To reframe the question of maximizing home runs, are the Sox putting enough runners on base to make the most of the homers they hit? According to Elias, they’re doing that better than most. Entering Sunday, the Sox ranked fifth in the majors in runs scored via home run at 44.6% The Reds ranked first at 49.9%.</p><p>“You want to touch pillows as often as possible,” the colorful Shomon said, referring to bases. “It’s something that we talk about as a group, finding a way. Whether that’s a hit by pitch, a walk, reaching on an error.</p><p>“But where you do see the offense falter a little bit is there is some swing and miss. Adjustments are certainly talked about, they’re worked on. Do they always show up? Not necessarily. But again, we have to lean on the things that we do well, and that’s forcing pitchers into the strike zone, driving up pitch counts and taking advantage of mistakes.”</p><p>Murakami, Montgomery and Vargas are doing just that. The last Sox trio with 30-plus homers was Carlos Quentin, Jermaine Dye and Jim Thome. In 2006, Joe Crede, Dye, Thome and Paul Konerko all hit at least 30. In 2004, Konerko, Carlos Lee and Jose Valentin did it.</p><p>What’s more, Murakami became just the fourth Japanese-born player in MLB history to hit 30 home runs, joining Shohei Ohtani (six times), Seiya Suzuki (2025) and Hideki Matsui (2004). The Sox’ season is historic locally and internationally.</p><p>And those homers could loom large in the final week of the season, when the Sox face the Royals and Rockies, who rank eighth and fourth, respectively, in most home runs allowed. What fortuitous timing for a team whose playoff push figures to go down to the wire.</p><p>But the Sox didn’t need any homers to beat the Twins. They led 5-1 when Grichuk homered to lead off the eighth inning, and Teel later launched a three-run shot. Before all that, Murakami had an RBI single, Sam Antonacci a two-run double and Grichuk added an RBI single. Vargas walked in a run, and Tristan Peters had a two-run double.</p><h3>Runs via home runs</h3><p>Entering Sunday, the White Sox ranked fifth in the majors in the percentage of runs scored via home runs, according to Elias.</p><p>1. Reds 49.9%</p><p>2. Mariners 47.8%</p><p>3. Yankees 47.0%</p><p>4. Cubs 45.1%</p><p>5. entries.title: At least 5 dead after Amazon cargo plane barrels off runway at Miami airport
entries.summary: <p>MIAMI — An Amazon cargo plane barreled off a runway at Miami International Airport on Sunday, killing at least five people and injuring five others as it struck vehicles and was engulfed in flames, authorities said.</p><p>The aircraft overran the runway around 2 p.m. after arriving from San Juan, Puerto Rico, and plowed across a road used by warehouse workers and other businesses that surround the airport. Five people were killed, three critically injured and two others hospitalized with less severe injuries, Miami-Dade County officials told a news conference.</p><p>Miami officials said Sunday afternoon that it was too soon to say whether the people who died were on board the plane or in the vehicles the plane hit.</p><p>The crash, which sent thick black smoke billowing into the sky, trapped the pilot and copilot in the cockpit and some occupants in cars, said Miami-Dade Rescue Fire Chief Ray Jadallah. The agency said crews also had to extricate a person who was trapped under a vehicle.</p><p>The crash halted flights at the busy travel hub for much of the afternoon. Some 200 emergency personnel responded, finding the plane with heavy flames and smoke from a complex engine compartment fire, the department said. Firefighters used foam from specialized airport firefighting units to extinguish the fire, and crews were still dealing with a fuel leak on the plane hours later.</p><p>The Prime Air plane came to rest beside a roadway near two semi-trucks, images showed. The aircraft appeared to be resting on its belly and was largely intact despite the fire.</p><p>The cause had yet to be determined, and it was not clear if weather had played a role. Thunderstorms and wind gusts up to 30 mph were recorded in the area at the time, according to the National Weather Service.</p><p>The flight had been operated by 21 Air, a cargo carrier based in North Carolina. The 32-year-old Boeing 767 was originally built to carry passengers and flew for several airlines for more than two decades before being converted to a cargo plane in 2015, according to flight-tracking site Flightradar24.</p><p>The National Transportation Safety Board said it was sending a team to Miami led by Chairwoman Jennifer Homendy to investigate.</p><p>Amazon said in a statement that it would cooperate with any investigation.</p><p>“We’re heartbroken to learn that five people lost their lives in today’s incident at Miami International Airport," the company said. “Our deepest sympathies go out to the families, loved ones, and all those affected by this devastating loss.”</p><p>Last year, a UPS plane crashed after losing its engine while accelerating down the runway at Louisville’s Muhammad Ali International Airport. The crash killed all three pilots and 12 people on the ground. Twenty-three more were injured.</p><p>Aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said that a 767 cargo aircraft would typically be staffed only by a pilot and copilot on domestic flights. A third pilot would be added for an international flight, and a long-haul international flight would require a fourth pilot.</p><p>Arroyo, a retired longtime United Airlines pilot, said he wants to know whether the Amazon plane landed in the touchdown zone of the runway, and if it was beyond that area why it didn’t simply abort that landing and go around to line up for another attempt. Typically, the landing zone is within the first 3,000 feet (914 meters) of a runway.</p><p>“Did the aircraft land within the required touchdown zone?" he asked. “If it did, what happened?”</p><p>Mary Schiavo, who is a pilot and former inspector general of the Transportation Department, said that video posted online of the landing shows the Amazon plane floating above the runway for an extended period without flaring the nose upward to force the main landing gear onto the ground.</p><p>“It didn’t touch down right away, and so it lost a lot of critical real estate by just continuing to float over the runway. It was literally still flying,” Schiavo said.</p><p>She noted the Miami airport is not equipped with arresting systems that the FAA says have been installed at more than 120 airports nationwide to safely stop planes that do go past the end of a runway. Those beds of lightweight, crushable material at the end of a runway have been credited by the FAA with helping save at least 497 lives aboard planes that overran runways.</p>

entries.summary: <p>A Springfield man was fatally shot Sunday in Austin on the West Side, according to Chicago police.</p><p>Jerome Kirk, 20, was sitting in a car in the 300 block of North Lamon Avenue at 12:15 p.m. when a person walked up to the vehicle and fired shots, according to police and the Cook County medical examiner's office. </p><p>Kirk was taken to Mt. entries.title: Notre Dame pours it on in second half to rout Wisconsin
entries.summary: <p>GREEN BAY, Wis.— Notre Dame coach Marcus Freeman knows Wisconsin coach Luke Fickell well enough to realize the Fighting Irish would face a bigger season-opening challenge than the recent results of these two teams suggested.</p><p>Freeman's team eventually responded.</p><p>CJ Carr threw two touchdown passes, Aneyas Williams ran for 90 yards and two more scores and No. 4 Notre Dame pulled away in the second half to beat Wisconsin 41-13 on Sunday night at Lambeau Field. Notre Dame led just 13-10 at halftime before dominating the final two periods.</p><p>“Human nature is maybe you look at somebody else’s record last year — and everybody has expectations on what you should be this year — to think this is how this game should go,” said Freeman, who played for Fickell at Ohio State and coached alongside him at Cincinnati. “I don't know how they thought it would go, but I wanted to make sure at halftime they knew it was going to be a babble and going to be a struggle. I told them that all week. Sometimes you don't believe it until you're in it.”</p><p>This was the first college football game at the home of the NFL’s Green Bay Packers since 2016, when Wisconsin upset a fifth-ranked LSU team 16-14. Wisconsin also hung around for a while in this one as a three-touchdown underdog as it attempts to bounce back from two straight losing seasons.</p><p>Notre Dame's first touchdown came on a 3-yard reception by Green Bay resident James Flanigan, whose father and grandfather (each named Jim Flanigan) both played for the Packers.</p><p>“There's three generations of Flanigans who have been on that field and made some plays,” Flanigan said. “That's really special.”</p><p>Carr went 19 of 29 for 239 yards. His other touchdown completion was a 28-yarder to Nolan James Jr. with 1:51 left.</p><p>The Irish entered this season pledging to leave no doubt about their College Football Playoff worthiness after getting left out of the field last year despite winning their last 10 regular-season games by double-digit margins.</p><p>But the Irish’s performance early on created plenty of doubt about how effectively they can run the ball without Heisman Trophy finalist Jeremiyah Love and Jadarian Price, the only two running backs selected in the first round of this year’s NFL draft. Notre Dame rushed for 111 yards on 32 carries — including just 29 yards o 16 attempts in the first half.</p><p>Notre Dame's offense eventually got in gear. The Irish scored touchdowns on each of their three second-half possessions.</p><p>“I don’t have a great explanation for the second half,” Fickell said. “I give them a lot of credit. We kind of held the energy and created a lot of momentum in the first half. In the second half, we could do none.”</p><p>Williams’ 3-yard touchdown run capped a 70-yard drive to open the second half. Colorado transfer DJ McKinney then intercepted Colton Joseph’s pass and ran untouched for a 55-yard touchdown to make it 27-10.</p><p>Gavin Lahm’s second field goal of the night cut Notre Dame’s lead to 27-13 near the end of the third, but Williams capped the Irish’s next drive with a 5-yard touchdown run and James completed the scoring in the closing minutes.</p><p>“We prepared for a battle,” Carr said. “We got a battle in the first half. We were really excited, I think, coming out of the second half because Free talks about there’s nothing great that comes from something that’s easy. We knew it was going to be a struggle. It's what we wanted, and (we) ended up finishing really strong."</p><p><b>The takeaway</b></p><p>Wisconsin: After adding 34 transfers, Wisconsin certainly looks better than it has the last couple of years. But the Badgers needed to play mistake-free football to have a shot at pulling the upset, and they instead had two turnovers that led to Notre Dame touchdowns.</p><p>Notre Dame: The Irish's defense could face some early adversity. The Irish lost preseason Associated Press All-America second-team safety Brauntae Johnson and defensive lineman Jason Onye to injuries during the game. Freeman had no update on either player after the game. Preseason AP All-America second-team linebacker Kyngstonn Viliamu-Asa didn't play as he continues to recover from a knee injury that ended his 2025 season early.</p><p>One positive development for Notre Dame came from Purdue transfer Spencer Porath, who made field goals of 52 and 26 yards in his Irish debut. Last season, Notre Dame didn’t make a field goal after Oct. 11.</p><p><b>Up next</b></p><p>Wisconsin: Hosts Western Illinois on Saturday.</p><p>Notre Dame: Hosts Rice on Saturday.</p>

entries.title: Former Bears FB Matt Suhey, member of 1985 championship team, dies at 68
entries.summary: <p>Former <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> fullback Matt Suhey, who played on their 1985 championship team, died Sunday at 68, the team confirmed. He scored the first touchdown in Super Bowl XX on an 11-yard run as they rolled to a 46-10 win to capture the only Lombardi Trophy in franchise history.</p><p>Suhey played a decade with the Bears in the 1980s, including eight years as the lead blocker for Hall of Fame running back Walter Payton. He was a key piece during their best run in modern history with five consecutive playoff appearances from 1984 through ’88.</p><p>There is a famous photo of Payton and Suhey at a practice in the spring of 1985 in which Suhey is lined up for a play and Payton is pulling his shorts down from behind with a big smile on his face. Former Sun-Times columnist Rick Telander <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/sports-saturday/2019/11/16/20967691/chicago-bears-iconic-photos-walter-payton-matt-suhey-blessing-curse-local-photographer-jim-maentanis" target="_blank" >wrote that they were “best buds”</a> and, “Their affection for each other would become clearest when Payton was dying of liver cancer and Suhey was there to soothe his friend and run interference for him against the swarming media horde.</p><p>The Bears drafted Suhey out of Penn State in the second round in 1980 and he went on to become one of their most celebrated players.</p><p>He played in every game as a rookie and was an incredibly reliable and durable player and appeared in 148 of a possible 152 games. He finished with 2,946 yards rushing and 20 touchdown runs, as well as 260 catches for 2,113 yards and five touchdowns. The Sun-Times ranked him No. 78 in its <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2019/9/5/20850765/the-100-greatest-bears-of-all-time" target="_blank" >100 Greatest Bears of All Time</a> for their 100th season in 2019.</p>

entries.title: Big Tobacco, toymakers pay for the harm they've caused. Why not gunmakers?
entries.summary: <p>The recent <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/31/washington-park-mass-shooting-chicago" >mass shooting</a> in Washington Park was, yet again, a reminder that despite our city's progress in reducing gun violence, the work is far from finished.</p><p>But as trauma surgeons at the University of Chicago Medical Center, we didn’t need a reminder: We anticipate and prepare for nights like Aug. 29.</p><p>Multiple operating rooms lie dormant, awaiting the victims who will eventually fill them. Trays are open to repair chests, abdomens and repair arteries. Coolers are stocked with blood — some drawn from the drives we organize knowing what the summer will entail.</p><p>The morning after the mass shooting in Washington Park, our facility was filled with residents and surgeons wearing scrubs spattered with blood. Their eyes were heavy from the controlled chaos of the night before when they tried to preserve the life of each patient who came through the doors.</p><p>We wish tending to more than 20 gunshot victims in a 12-hour period was an anomaly.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-bb0000" name="module-bb0000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Commentary bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Commentary</h2></div> </div><p>While we healthcare workers love our jobs, seeing the effects of human-induced violence leaves us reeling with secondary trauma and paranoia. We are tired. We are traumatized. We've had enough.</p><p>Chicago's <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/01/01/chicago-crime-murder-homicide-shooting-president-trump-mayor-johnson" >historic reductions</a> in gun violence and murders didn't happen by accident, or by the swiftness of our scalpel. Rather, it was the result of investments in community violence intervention programs that identify the highest-risk individuals and city blocks, stop conflicts before they escalate and provide the resources that prevent shootings.</p><p>These successes are why we have grown weary of what follows on nights like Aug. 29: reflexive calls for law and order, demands to be "tougher" on crime, and proposals to repeal Illinois' Safety, Accountability, Fairness and Equity-Today, or SAFE-T, Act. Such political grandstanding centers solutions the evidence does not support. The outcries produce nothing to prevent the next tragedy.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/09/01/mass-shooting-washington-park-waller-johnson" >culprits behind</a> the mass shooting in Washington Park must be brought to justice. But real accountability can't begin and end with an arrest. Responsibility must extend to the conditions that produce the violence: economic desperation, adverse childhood experiences and the collapse of social infrastructure in communities that have been left behind. Responsibility must also extend to the gun manufacturers whose products make mass injury not just possible but routine.</p><p>Victims who survive will struggle with their injuries while paying their medical bills. Those with private health insurance will shoulder the costs hospitals must recoup, and taxpayers will subsidize the consequences of firearm manufacturers' for-profit ventures. Everyone pays for gun violence — victims, families, communities, healthcare providers — except those who make money off the production of the lethal weapons.</p><p>Since 2005, firearm manufacturers have been shielded from most civil liability under the Protection in Lawful Commerce in Arms Act.</p><h3>Evading responsibility</h3><p>Other industries have rightly paid the price when their products caused serious harm:</p><p>Tobacco manufacturers were <a class="Link" href="https://www.fightcancer.org/policy-resources/history-racketeering-lawsuit-against-tobacco-industry-guilty-deceiving-american" target="_blank" >hit</a> with federal racketeering convictions, multibillion-dollar settlements and mandates for their ad campaigns.</p><p>Sales and production of metal-tipped lawn darts were <a class="Link" href="https://www.cpsc.gov/Newsroom/News-Releases/1997/Following-Recent-Injury-CPSC-Reissues-Warning-Lawn-Darts-Are-Banned-and-Should-Be-Destroyed" target="_blank" >banned</a> after three children were killed.</p><p>Buckyballs <a class="Link" href="https://www.inc.com/magazine/201210/april-joyner/case-study-government-regulators-buckyballs.html" target="_blank" >were pulled from shelves</a> by the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission after 12 surgeries were performed on children and teens who swallowed pieces of the toy.</p><p>Four Loko beverages were <a class="Link" href="https://www.nbcchicago.com/news/local/fda-expected-to-ban-caffeinated-alcoholic-drinks/2090061/" target="_blank" >reformulated</a> under intense pressure from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration after people were hospitalized.</p><p>Kinder Surprise eggs are <a class="Link" href="https://www.cpsc.gov/Newsroom/News-Releases/2006/CPSC-Warns-of-Banned-Kinder-Chocolate-Eggs-Containing-Toys-Which-Can-Pose-Choking-Aspiration-Hazards-to-Young-Children" target="_blank" >still banned for sale and import</a> in the United States due to choking hazards.</p><p>Yet, gun manufacturers evade responsibility even though <a class="Link" href="https://www.apha.org/topics-and-issues/gun-violence" target="_blank" >firearms kill 48,000 Americans</a> every year and are the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/10/17/23919379/deaths-children-teens-leading-cause-firearms-homicide-suicide-prevention-the-conversation" >leading cause</a> of death for children and teenagers.</p><p>Nearly $20 billion a year is spent in law enforcement response and recovery expenses tied to gun violence in Illinois.</p><p>Illinois' proposed <a class="Link" href="https://www.ilga.gov/Legislation/BillStatus?DocTypeID=HB&DocNum=3320&GAID=18&SessionID=114&LegID=161810" target="_blank" >Responsibility in Firearms Legislation Act</a> creates an accountability that is long overdue. Under the <a class="Link" href="https://www.cbsnews.com/chicago/news/rifl-act-springfield-gun-violence/" target="_blank" >legislation</a>, firearm manufacturers in Illinois would be required to obtain a state license. Money collected from the licensing fees would go into a dedicated fund to help gun violence victims.</p><p>Perhaps requiring manufacturers to bear a fraction of the costs their products create will help communities build on their efforts to keep residents safe. Perhaps the financial incentive will drive what moral obligation has not: safer distribution practices, investment in violence prevention and innovation in product design. Perhaps Chicago might yet become what we believe it can be — the safest big city in America.</p><p>We will continue to do our part. We will stock the coolers and prep the rooms. We will stand ready in the trauma center and treat every gunshot victim. We will support efforts to stop the bloodshed and resist the theater of toughness.</p><p>But at the end of every night like the tragic evening of Aug. 29, we ask our city and state stakeholders the same question patients ask us: “Did we do everything we could to save them?”</p><p><i>Dr. Anthony Douglas is a surgical resident and public health practitioner at the University of Chicago Medical Center.</i></p><p><i>Dr. Selwyn Rogers Jr. is the founding director and chief of trauma and acute care surgery at the University of Chicago Medical Center. He is the author of  the book "Healing the Gun Violence Epidemic."</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-c80000" name="module-c80000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Weariness, wariness likely to follow blue-collar union voters to the polls
entries.summary: <p>When union workers and their families gather this Labor Day, some may ponder <a class="Link" href="https://www.hks.harvard.edu/publications/are-you-better-you-were-4-years-ago" target="_blank" >Ronald Reagan’s memorable refrain</a>, “Are you better off now than you were four years ago?”</p><p>All workers — unionized or not — are dealing with higher prices for <a class="Link" href="https://www.consumeraffairs.com/news/affordability-here-are-the-costs-causing-the-most-pain-082826.html" target="_blank" >food and gasoline</a>.</p><p>For America’s unionized workforce, the overall state of the economy is bleak. Threats from <a class="Link" href="https://www.cbsnews.com/news/bill-gates-ai-jobs-warning/" target="_blank" >artificial intelligence </a>and robotics abound. <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/07/business/economy/trump-foreign-investment.html" target="_blank" >Pledges by U.S. and international corporations</a> to invest in new plants remain largely pledges. The <a class="Link" href="https://www.nbcnews.com/data-graphics/2025-doge-trump-administration-federal-job-cuts-total-rcna588589" target="_blank" >roughly 400,000 federal job cuts</a> during President Donald Trump’s second term have disrupted lives. Many of these jobs were previously represented by labor unions.</p><p>As a <a class="Link" href="https://www.press.uillinois.edu/books/?id=65nfk8hb9780252044397" target="_blank" >labor studies scholar</a>, I believe weariness and wariness will accompany blue-collar voters to the polls in November. As such, the candidates who have practical ideas for turning the economy around and exhibit empathy for Americans worried about how to pay their bills could receive the bulk of the union vote.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-390000" name="module-390000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Commentary bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Commentary</h2></div> </div><p>Over generations, the majority of <a class="Link" href="https://www.americanprogressaction.org/article/since-2020-union-member-support-for-democrats-has-increased/" target="_blank" >union members have sided with Democratic candidates</a>, even if that support has <a class="Link" href="https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/hard-hat-riot-1970-pitted-construction-workers-against-anti-war-protestors-180974831/" target="_blank" >wavered since the 1970s</a>.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2024/10/17/key-facts-about-union-members-and-the-2024-election/" target="_blank" >2024 presidential campaign</a> was <a class="Link" href="https://www.americanprogressaction.org/article/while-other-voters-moved-away-from-the-democrats-union-members-shifted-toward-harris-in-2024/" target="_blank" >no exception</a>. The majority of union members voted for Democratic candidates, but at a far lower rate than in the 1960s.</p><p>Why does this matter in 2026?</p><p>Union voters <a class="Link" href="https://www.bls.gov/news.release/pdf/union2.pdf" target="_blank" >play a bigger role in Michigan, Pennsylvania and Nevada</a>, three swing states where the share of voters who belong to unions is above the national average of 10%. In closely contested U.S. House and Senate races, even a small shift in union votes could influence the outcome.</p><p>In Illinois, where <a class="Link" href="https://theconversation.com/labor-day-and-may-day-emerged-from-the-movement-for-a-shorter-workday-in-industrial-america-262379" target="_blank" >the 1894 Pullman strike spurred the creation of Labor Day</a>, the AFL-CIO endorsed all but a small number of Democrats in state legislative races this year. It’s worth noting that <a class="Link" href="https://capitolnewsillinois.com/news/illinois-afl-cio-issues-endorsements-after-all/" target="_blank" >who the Illinois AFL-CIO endorses</a> in November elections represents a barometer of where the state’s labor vote is likely to go.</p><p>How large is the union vote?</p><p>The latest <a class="Link" href="https://www.bls.gov/news.release/union2.nr0.htm" target="_blank" >Bureau of Labor Statistics figures</a> show the percentage of U.S. unionized workers has fallen over the past four decades.</p><p>In 1983, 20.1% of U.S. workers were represented by a union. In 2025, the rate was 10%, or 14.7 million people. Union membership among public sector workers (32.9%) is more than five times higher than that of private sector workers (5.9%). In close elections, the volatility of these voting blocs matters.</p><p>During the 2024 presidential campaign, <a class="Link" href="https://www.presidency.ucsb.edu/documents/2024-republican-party-platform" target="_blank" >Trump promised to reduce consumer prices</a>, bring back <a class="Link" href="https://www.brookings.edu/events/can-trump-bring-manufacturing-back-to-the-us/" target="_blank" >manufacturing jobs</a> and respect workers’ rights.</p><p>As the midterm elections approach, I believe the president’s performance on these issues in the eyes of union voters will determine which party controls the U.S. House and Senate. And the signs are not promising for Trump, with recent polls indicating <a class="Link" href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/business/2026/06/12/union-voters-are-mad-trump-frustrated-with-democrats-ahead-midterms/" target="_blank" >the president’s support among union households</a> is eroding.</p><p>The U.S. economy has <a class="Link" href="https://www.marketplace.org/story/2026/07/28/is-trumps-aggressive-trade-policy-reshoring-factory-jobs" target="_blank" >lost 75,000 manufacturing jobs</a> since January 2025, a 0.6% decline. These jobs have steadily declined since the 1980s, so Trump’s policies are not solely to blame.</p><p>Furthermore, <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2025/03/13/business/economy/trump-tariff-timeline.html" target="_blank" >Trump’s off-again, on-again tariffs</a> may help some U.S. manufacturers. That’s because tariffs can erase the advantages of low-cost overseas labor. As <a class="Link" href="https://www.marketplace.org/story/2026/07/28/is-trumps-aggressive-trade-policy-reshoring-factory-jobs" target="_blank" >economist Laura Veldkamp noted</a> in July, Trump’s tariffs “made it more profitable for American manufacturers to set up and produce here.”</p><p>The bigger problem, though, is even if some manufacturing returns to the U.S., the work will likely be done with the latest manufacturing technologies, which tend to reduce the need for workers. That does not bode well for <a class="Link" href="https://www.bls.gov/careeroutlook/2026/article/manufacturing.htm" target="_blank" >significant job creation</a>.</p><p> In July, Moody’s <a class="Link" href="https://www.marketplace.org/story/2026/07/28/is-trumps-aggressive-trade-policy-reshoring-factory-jobs" target="_blank" >financial analyst Mark Zandi told Marketplace</a> that more manufacturing output “doesn’t translate into jobs.” He explained there has been more activity in the tech sector and in the defense-aerospace industries, but “these factories just don’t employ a lot of people.”</p><p>Additionally, Trump has not established a clear plan to <a class="Link" href="https://www.ap.org/news-highlights/elections/2026/trump-has-a-new-surprising-take-on-the-higher-cost-of-living-i-love-the-inflation/" target="_blank" >lower inflation</a>. The <a class="Link" href="https://www.ers.usda.gov/data-products/food-price-outlook/summary-findings" target="_blank" >U.S. Department of Agriculture reports</a> food prices last July were up 3% from July 2025. This increase is slightly above the historical average.</p><h3>Generational suffering</h3><p>There’s one more factor to consider. <a class="Link" href="https://billmoyers.com/story/working-class-voters-books/" target="_blank" >Many older blue-collar workers</a> — many of them former union members — across New England, the Great Lakes, Ohio and western Pennsylvania remain angry about the epic <a class="Link" href="https://www.westfield.ma.edu/historical-journal/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/2018-Winter-Forrant-The-Rise-and-Demise-of-the-Connecticut-River-Valley%E2%80%99s-Industrial-Economy.pdf" target="_blank" >industrial collapse of the 1970s and 1980s</a>.</p><p>This kind of <a class="Link" href="https://www.westfield.ma.edu/historical-journal/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/2018-Winter-Forrant-The-Rise-and-Demise-of-the-Connecticut-River-Valley%E2%80%99s-Industrial-Economy.pdf" target="_blank" >generational suffering</a> can show up in the voting booth in a big way. And I don’t think voter surveys and polls are able to measure the depths of this rage.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://www.congress.gov/bill/95th-congress/senate-bill/2640" target="_blank" >Civil Service Reform Act of 1978</a> allowed government workers to unionize. But a March 2025 White House announcement said <a class="Link" href="https://www.whitehouse.gov/fact-sheets/2025/03/fact-sheet-president-donald-j-trump-exempts-agencies-with-national-security-missions-from-federal-collective-bargaining-requirements/" target="_blank" >the legislation had enabled</a> “hostile Federal unions to obstruct agency management.”</p><p>Through an <a class="Link" href="https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/03/exclusions-from-federal-labor-management-relations-programs/" target="_blank" >executive order</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://www.npr.org/2025/12/18/nx-s1-5626822/trump-federal-workers-firing-civil-servants" target="_blank" >mass layoffs across the federal workforce</a> in 2025, Trump has presided over a dramatic change in <a class="Link" href="https://thehill.com/homenews/administration/5218975-trump-administration-moves-to-end-union-rights-for-many-federal-workers/" target="_blank" >public sector collective bargaining</a> in Washington, D.C.</p><p>Offering guidance on the 2025 executive order, the <a class="Link" href="https://www.opm.gov/chcoc/latest-memos/guidance-on-executive-order-exclusions-from-federal-labor-management-programs.pdf" target="_blank" >U.S. Office of Personnel Management directed federal agencies</a> to end their collective bargaining agreement.</p><p>In response, the American Federation of Government Employees <a class="Link" href="https://thehill.com/homenews/administration/5218975-trump-administration-moves-to-end-union-rights-for-many-federal-workers/" target="_blank" >condemned the action in an email to its members</a>, saying the Trump administration was “illegally strip(ping) collective bargaining rights from hundreds of thousands of federal workers.”</p><p>Federal unions have <a class="Link" href="https://www.afge.org/article/summary-of-afge-lawsuits-against-trump--how-litigation-works-2/" target="_blank" >challenged the White House’s March 2025 executive order</a>. In 2026, independent arbitrators have also ruled against the administration’s efforts to circumvent labor agreements with some <a class="Link" href="https://federalnewsnetwork.com/workforce-rightsgovernance/2026/08/losses-keep-piling-up-for-trump-administration-over-handling-of-rto-mandate/" target="_blank" >federal workers</a>. And in June, a federal judge in Massachusetts <a class="Link" href="https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.mad.299038/gov.uscourts.mad.299038.41.0.pdf" target="_blank" >struck down an effort by the Trump administration</a> to exercise control over union elections at federal agencies.</p><p>Whether unionized industrial workers support their public sector counterparts remains to be seen.</p><p><i>Robert Forrant is professor of U.S. history and labor studies at University of Massachusetts Lowell.</i></p><p><i>This </i><a class="Link" href="https://theconversation.com/labor-votes-discontent-will-accompany-blue-collar-voters-to-the-polls-in-the-midterms-285564" target="_blank" ><i>article</i></a><i> was originally published on </i><a class="Link" href="https://theconversation.com/us" target="_blank" ><i>theconversation.com</i></a><i>.</i></p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-860000" name="html-embed-module-860000"></a><iframe src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/285564/count.gif?distributor=republish-lightbox-advanced" width="1" height="1" style="border: none !important" referrerpolicy="no-referrer-when-downgrade"></iframe> </div> </div><p></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-640000" name="module-640000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Steinem guided my way
entries.summary: <p>My New Trier High School Class of 1972 had to write a major research paper on a topic of our choice during our junior year. I decided to write about the modern women's liberation movement. My sources were the works of feminist thinkers and artists. Many of my classmates knew me as a "women's libber," which was not necessarily a term of endearment.</p><p>Shortly after senior year, <i>Ms.</i> magazine hit the newsstands. It was the first women's magazine run entirely by women, with content that did not include recipes, household cleaning tips and advice columns. I was excited, scared, not sure who I was or what I wanted out of life as I went off for college. But I had <i>Ms.</i> magazine in my hand, and I knew one thing: I was a feminist.</p><p>And as a feminist, I could have a career and get married and have children — or not— because <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/obituaries/2026/09/03/gloria-steinem-a-potent-voice-of-us-feminism-and-co-founder-of-ms-magazine-dies-at-92" >Gloria Steinem</a> said so. She was a journalist, philosopher, activist, publisher and an inspiration to me every day.</p><p>I majored in women's history at Duke University and secured an internship at the National Women's Political Caucus, an organization Steinem co-founded. Soon after, I became a lobbyist for the National Organization for Women, and my first real boyfriend had been an organizer with Ralph Nader in Michigan. He was very supportive of my feminist ways, as long as they didn't interfere with his dreams.</p><p>After seven years in Washington, D.C., I met and got some advice from a woman who was a lawyer, activist and lesbian. She told me that I could have a great career as a nonprofit leader if that's what I wanted. But she said if I wanted to go into business, I had to go for it immediately. In three to four years, I'd be too old and experienced for an entry-level job and would never be able to break into corporate America, she told me.</p><p>I moved back to Chicago, got a job at Leo Burnett, got married, had children and hung on to my feminist values. I married a man who accepted me for who I am and did not think his life and his dreams were more important than mine.</p><p>I can't think of another public figure who had more impact on my life than Steinem. She was there for me at every important move, decision and action. Rest in peace my friend who I never met. I'm forever grateful for your life and its impact on mine.</p><p><i>Nina Abnee, Avondale</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-e90000" name="module-e90000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Chicago’s star turn</h3><p>This fall, I'll begin production on a <a class="Link" href="https://www.zmarcproductions.com/films/castaway" target="_blank" >short film</a> with a diverse cast and crew entirely from the Chicago area, including the film’s creator and director, Nathan L. Marquez. It's a relief knowing there are no flights to book. Every actor lives within an hour of set. Every filming location is within driving distance. Ten years ago that would have been a compromise. Today it's a flex.</p><p>As an independent filmmaker, I'm seeing a revival in the Midwest. For a growing number of productions and independent storytellers, Chicago isn't the alternative to Hollywood. It's the first call.</p><p>People often forget Chicago was a hub for the film industry before Los Angeles. Through film, the city made an indelible mark on the world, but then the business went West, chasing weather and cheap land.</p><p>In recent years, I've seen a resurgence like never before, incentivizing independent filmmakers to return to this great city and nurture homegrown talent.</p><p>Last year, Gov. JB Pritzker signed an expansion of the <a class="Link" href="https://dceo.illinois.gov/whyillinois/film/filmtaxcredit.html" target="_blank" >Illinois Film Production Tax Credit Act</a>, offering producers credit of 35% of all qualified Illinois spending.</p><p>There's also 5% additional credit available for productions that meet sustainability certification requirements. Best of all, the minimum spending amount to qualify was lowered to $100,000 for productions over 30 minutes and $50,000 for productions under 30 minutes.</p><p>That number isn't aimed at Dick Wolf-sized productions. It's aimed at independent production companies like mine and independent producers with scripts waiting to be brought to life.</p><p>As a result, Illinois film production spending hit a <a class="Link" href="https://www.illinoisproduction.org/" target="_blank" >record</a> $703 million in 2025, up 25% from 2019. Industry wages <a class="Link" href="https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/business/business-news/hollywood-spending-illinois-1236539967/" target="_blank" >rose</a> from $350 million to $401 million, and local hires climbed from 15,200 to 18,100.</p><p>I believe the renaissance for independent Chicago storytelling is beginning, through the emerging independent film scene. With these incentives, the settings, stars and storytellers from the Chicago area are finally being spotlighted once again.</p><p><i>Thomas Z. Seffernick, founder, Z Marc Productions</i></p><h3>Let them build</h3><p>As a young zoning lawyer in 1980, I witnessed the battle over proposed development at Sheridan Road and Thorndale Avenue.</p><p>Now as an Edgewater resident, I experience the results of NIMBY’s success in that fight: a lushly landscaped pocket park that few people use and no woman will cross at night fearing what might lurk in the bushes. Public safety would have been better served by more housing and foot traffic.</p><p>The neighborhood group <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/09/01/battle-emanuel-congregation-fern-hill-lakefront-home-edgewater" >protesting</a> Emanuel Congregation's mixed-use development has also opposed every other proposal to create desperately needed housing. Apparently, the ideal neighborhood is one that let them in and then slammed the door behind them.</p><p>Friends of the Parks is organized to maximize park area in the city. This worthy goal seems to blind the group to the fact that Edgewater isn’t short of parks; it’s short of housing.</p><p>Legislation known as <a class="Link" href="https://d38cycikt2ca4e.cloudfront.net/documents/YIGBY_SB635_-_Status_Update_5.29.26.pdf" target="_blank" >YIGBY</a> (Yes In God’s Back Yard) would allow houses of worship to build housing on their spare land without being subjected to the death by a thousand cuts now facing Emanuel Congregation. I urge Illinois lawmakers to pass the legislation, and I urge my neighbors to get the hell out of the way.</p><p><i>Kelly Kleiman, Edgewater</i></p>

entries.title: If Bears can't answer abounding questions about their defense, they're headed for a .500 season
entries.summary: <p>The thought of a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> season full of shootouts and three-hour frenzies in which anything can happen is thrilling. It wasn’t that long ago that their games were unwatchable — Anybody remember the 6-3 loss to the Seahawks in 2024? — so a weekly race to 40 points sounds entertaining.</p><p>It is not, however, the typical formula to compete for a championship.</p><p>The closer the Bears get to their season opener Sunday at the Panthers, the harder it is to envision their defense taking them where they want to go. They have the potential to be an overwhelming offense if quarterback <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2024/08/30/caleb-williams-wins-bears-over-with-rare-talent-but-even-rarer-people-skills" >Caleb Williams</a> continues his upward trajectory under coach <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/09/01/the-bears-and-their-fans-needed-a-truth-teller-they-got-one-in-new-coach-ben-johnson" >Ben Johnson</a>, and that side of the ball is loaded with playmakers, but it can’t compensate for what they’re missing defensively.</p><p>Being great on one side of the ball and bad on the other usually balances out. It’s the equation to finish around .500.</p><p>Over the last four seasons, 14 of the 20 teams that reached the conference championship game had finished in the top of the NFL in total defense during the regular season. The last four Super Bowls were played between teams that finished 11th or higher.</p><p>Total defense is just one statistic, but it’s fairly telling: How easy is it for opposing offenses to move the ball on you? Teams that make it tough tend to win.</p><p>The Bears proved last season there are exceptions to that logic and reached the divisional round despite finishing 29th in yards allowed. They weren’t very good in the two basic tasks every defense seeks to accomplish, shutting down the run and disrupting opposing quarterbacks, but led the NFL in takeaways and were middle of the pack in red-zone defense.</p><p>They also took some heat off their defense by finishing sixth in total offense.</p><p>There wasn’t much fuss about allowing 42 points to the Bengals, for example, because the Bears piled up 47. Near the end of the season, though, those deficiencies glared in a 42-38 loss to the 49ers.</p><p>It’s a hard way to live, and the Bears know it.</p><p>Johnson has mentioned multiple times this offseason that there’s some randomness to takeaways and teams can’t count on getting them. Cornerback Jaylon Johnson said the blueprint can’t be to beat teams 40-35, calling it “unacceptable.”</p><p>Yet with everyone at Halas Hall grasping that reality, the Bears made only a halfhearted effort to fix it.</p><p>Their only major move in free agency or the trade market was to sign former Seahawks safety Coby Bryant, and that blew up on them when Bryant suffered a potentially season-ending knee injury in training camp. They also invested their first-round draft pick, No. 25 overall, in starting safety Dillon Thieneman.</p><p>The goal, they’ve said, is to find improvement from within. Players who haven’t produced somehow will start producing. The defensive coaches somehow will coach better, is if coordinator Dennis Allen and his staff weren’t already staying up late trying to solve those problems.</p><p>All of that is why there’s lingering doubt about the Bears nationally.</p><p>They’re 15th in odds to win the championship, and the over-under on their win total is 9.5. ESPN’s power rankings have them 12th, behind the Packers and Lions. And for all the whining Jaguars coach Liam Coen did about the NFL’s official website hyping Williams, its panel of voters picked the Bears to miss the playoffs.</p><p>The Bears will try to prove everyone wrong with a patchwork starting lineup to begin the season. That requires a lot of hope, and hope is not a plan.</p><p>They’ve replaced Bryant with Xavier Woods, a journeyman who was out of the league a month ago. Opposite defensive end Montez Sweat, they’re likely to start Austin Booker, a former fifth-rounder who has six sacks in 27 career games, over pricy 2025 signee Dayo Odeyingbo. With nickel cornerback Kyler Gordon hurt (again), they’re turning to rookie Malik Muhammad, a fourth-rounder who was the 16th player picked at his position and played mostly on the outside in college.</p><p>Additionally in the “hope” category, the Bears are banking on defensive tackle Grady Jarrett getting healthier at 33. They dealt fellow tackle Gervon Dexter to the Falcons and believe they’ll get more out of Kentavius Street, who is on his fourth team in five seasons. And they’re still waiting on beleaguered cornerback Tyrique Stevenson to figure it out.</p><p>There’s simply too much uncertainty on defense to justify optimism.</p><p>While it’s fair to question general manager Ryan Poles’ spending or Allen’s strategy, this problem ultimately lands on Johnson’s desk. Predecessors Matt Eberflus and Matt Nagy showed no ability to problem solve on the side of the ball that wasn’t their specialty, and he must succeed where they failed.</p><p>He dreams of breaking the 2013 Broncos’ scoring record of 37.9 points per game and that’s a great ambition, but the asterisk on that team is that it ran into the top-ranked Seahawks defense in the Super Bowl and got destroyed. Truly great teams tend to be strong on both sides of the ball, and those that are good at only one often end up in the dreaded middle.</p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Boyfriend wants to live with her, but not with her son
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I'm a single mother of an 18-year-old son with autism. I have known "Cliff" for more than 20 years. We live on opposite coasts. I want to be with him and he with me, though he doesn't want my son to live with us at this time. He wants it to be just the two of us for a while. Abby, my son is not able to live on his own. Do you have any advice as to what to do? — <i>CLUELESS IN THE WEST</i></p><p><b>DEAR CLUELESS:</b> It troubles me that Cliff is already trying to exclude your son from the equation. What exactly does he expect you to do with your son during this "honeymoon" period, and how long does he think it should last? It is important that you find out before this romance goes any further. What alternative living arrangements does Cliff have in mind for your son, what will they cost and who will be expected to pay for them?</p><p>You didn't mention how functional your son is, or how he interacts with others. Because he is 18, it's time to start thinking ahead regardless of Cliff. What will become of your son if something should happen to you? Would he be cared for by other relatives? Would a group living arrangement work for him?</p><p>Some developmentally disabled individuals thrive when they have social interaction and some kind of work to do. Before you start planning your love life, you need to address these issues. The Autism Society of America (autismsociety.org) may be able to help you navigate them.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My wife passed away unexpectedly while we were in Europe. I phoned several people in the U.S. to let them know and asked that they let others know. Someone in my wife's hometown posted the news to Facebook barely six hours after I had found her. My grief at the time was so great that I could not respond, as I was dealing with getting her remains back home. This has bothered me ever since that horrible day.</p><p>I sent the person a message, telling him I felt he had been disrespectful to me and my children. He replied that he had been so sad to learn that my wife had died that he felt compelled to post it to Facebook. (He did admit that his timing was bad.) I know I need to move on, and this person will definitely be left behind.</p><p>Is posting to social media acceptable before the family has had a chance to write an obituary and publish it? These platforms are public forums and should follow the normal rules of etiquette regarding respecting the family's privacy. — <i>MOURNING WIDOWER</i></p><p><b>DEAR MOURNING WIDOWER:</b> Please accept my sincere condolences on your wife's passing. The acquaintance who posted to Facebook committed a serious social media faux pas. It is never acceptable to make any public announcement of a person's death before the immediate family has done so. Still worse is the fact that he didn't wait for 24 hours before rushing to his keyboard. It appears you were never close with this self-appointed town crier, and I don't blame you for deciding you never will be.</p><p><b>DEAR READERS:</b> Have a safe and happy Labor Day! — <i>LOVE, ABBY</i></p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>
entries.author: Abigail Van Buren

entries.title: Lincoln's blood-stained gloves from his assassination resurface in California museum
entries.summary: <p>After being auctioned last year, blood-stained gloves Abraham Lincoln had when he was assassinated and that once were showcased at his presidential museum in Springfield have now turned up about 2,000 miles away in southern California.</p><p>The rare artifact, which was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2025/05/21/rare-abraham-lincoln-artifacts-sell-for-nearly-8-million-at-chicago-auction" >sold</a> last year to a mystery buyer for $1.5 million, is being exhibited at the Ronald Reagan Presidential Library and Museum until mid-September. It’s part of a <a class="Link" href="https://www.reaganfoundation.org/library-museum/special-exhibits/america-250" target="_blank" ><u>display</u></a> at the Simi Valley, Calif., museum commemorating America’s semiquincentennial.</p><p>It’s still unclear who bought the gloves.</p><p>But the fact they are back in a museum, even if for just a short time, represents the latest wrinkle in a saga over a tranche of prized Lincoln showpieces once intended to be permanently housed at the Abraham Lincoln Presidential Library and Museum in his hometown.</p><p>The gloves — and a now-discredited stovepipe hat originally touted as one belonging to Lincoln himself — were part of a $25 million acquisition of Lincoln artifacts in 2007 by a foundation established to stock the then-newly opened, state-run museum with antiquities tied to the 16th president.</p><p>But that collection was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/metro-state/2022/11/3/23439149/lincoln-artifacts-springfield-museum-feud" >carted</a> away in 2022 after relations between the Lincoln Presidential Foundation and museum soured, and items like the gloves were later auctioned off to help pay lingering debt tied to the original acquisition.</p><p>The fact the gloves have re-emerged in a West Coast museum may be a loss for Illinois residents who once could view them in Springfield, but one of the country’s top historical artifact experts says it’s still a win for the general public.</p><p>“It's quite obvious to me that the gloves were purchased by a private collector who is steeped in history and is eager to have them exhibited and shown to the public, which I think is a very positive thing,” said Marsha Malinowski, a nationally known historic books and manuscripts expert in New York City.</p><p>And the gloves, by far, have been one of the most popular draws this summer at the Reagan museum.</p><p>“It's the first case people want to see, and it's actually about halfway through the exhibition,” said Melissa Giller, who heads marketing and programming for the Ronald Reagan Presidential Foundation and Institute. “To see them in front of you really brings history to life in a way that reading a book or seeing a documentary can't.”</p><h3><b>Gloves were to have been owned by the state</b></h3><p>The<a class="Link" href="https://freemansauction.com/auction/6441-lincolns-legacy-historic-americana-from-the-life-of-abraham-lincoln/lot/114" target="_blank" ><u> once-ivory gloves</u></a> have yellowed over time, the kidskin leather flaking and cracking in some areas. But apart from the elastic bands at the wrist coming apart, the gloves have mostly stayed intact and bear unmistakable splotches of brown blood stains near the right thumb and the base of the left glove.</p><p>The 16th president was carrying them in his left coat pocket when he attended the comedic play, “Our American Cousin,” at Ford’s Theater in Washington, D.C., on April 14, 1865. As the play entered its third act, actor and Confederate sympathizer John Wilkes Booth fatally shot Lincoln in the back of the head.</p><p>It didn’t take long before Lincoln’s coat became soaked in blood. After he died the following morning, his coat, with the gloves still in the left pocket, was given to his eldest son, Robert Todd Lincoln, who then passed it on to his mother, Mary Todd Lincoln. After struggling financially, the president’s widow sold the gloves in 1868 to a family friend and collector of presidential memorabilia, Captain Benjamin Richardson.</p><p>In 1990, California-based Lincoln collector Louise Taper purchased the gloves from a descendant of Richardson’s. She held on to the gloves until 2007, when she sold it and other Lincoln items she owned to the foundation.</p><p>The intention originally was to transfer ownership of the gloves and other pieces of Taper’s collection to the Lincoln museum once a $23 million loan to acquire the items was repaid, but that transfer never happened.</p><p>Instead, the museum’s relationship with the foundation turned contentious, in part, over friction regarding the authenticity of a stovepipe hat that was regarded as the most valuable piece in the Taper trove.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div Cornelius, former curator of the Lincoln Collection at the Abraham Lincoln Presidential Library and Museum in Springfield shows the Abraham Lincoln hat in the museum’s collection in 2012. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Sun-Times file photo</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The hat was billed to be one of only three surviving hats once worn by Lincoln and at one point was appraised at $6.5 million. Both the Lincoln foundation and museum contended the hat had been gifted by Lincoln as a show of appreciation to a southern Illinois farmer and then passed down to the farmer’s son, Elbert Waller, who was a one-time Illinois legislator.</p><p>But the Chicago Sun-Times first <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2012/4/18/18533798/was-famous-stovepipe-hat-really-abe-lincoln-s" target="_blank" >disclosed</a> serious questions about its authenticity in 2012, unleashing an uproar that eventually led the museum to remove the hat from public display and the foundation to secretly and unsuccessfully test it for signs of Lincoln’s DNA.</p><p>A 2019 <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/politics/2019/12/23/report-no-evidence-disputed-hat-belonged-to-lincoln" target="_blank" >report</a> by Illinois’ then-state historian Samuel Wheeler stopped short of concluding the hat was a fake but laid out a series of previously unknown details that cast far deeper doubts about its authenticity. The report said the hat did not appear to be in Lincoln’s size, that it was once sold to a downstate antique shop for just $1 by Waller’s widow, and descendants of the hat’s original owner were unaware of its purported Lincoln lineage.</p><p>The hat’s squishy provenance hindered the foundation’s ability to raise money, prompting the organization to turn to the Illinois General Assembly for help in retiring what then was a $9 million debt from acquiring Taper’s collection. But that legislative effort failed in 2019.</p><p>In 2022, the Taper collection was transferred out of the Lincoln museum and, after over a century of changing hands, the gloves were auctioned in Chicago in May 2025.</p><p>Before the gloves were sold to an anonymous buyer, Taper told WBEZ she was “appalled” that more than 140 of her former Lincoln relics were being “dispersed to the wind.” Her wish, when selling to the foundation, was for the historical items to “reside in a place for the public to enjoy and learn from.”</p><p>“Never would I have thought that a foundation representing a museum would act separately and take everything away and put it up for sale,” Taper told WBEZ last year.</p><h3><b>Buyer’s identity still a mystery</b></h3><p>The Reagan Museum had been working on the America 250 exhibit for about a year and a half before it opened May 22. For the Civil War portion of the exhibit, Giller said the museum was able to acquire an actual cannon used by Union soldiers during the Battle of Gettysburg.</p><p>But she said they wanted more items related to Lincoln. So, the museum staff got in touch with Christie’s Auction House, which connected them to someone who had recently purchased Lincoln’s presidential campaign buttons.</p><p>“The person said to us … ‘By the way, if you're interested in more items, I also have the gloves he was wearing on the night he was assassinated that have his blood stains on them, and the handkerchief that was in his pocket. Would you like those?’” Giller said.</p><p>Giller declined to identify the gloves’ owner, who sought anonymity while loaning the item to the Reagan museum until the close of its exhibit Sept. 13.</p><p>That the gloves would be one of the most popular items now on display at the Reagan museum makes sense to Jacob Friefeld, director of the Center of Lincoln Studies at the University of Illinois Springfield. Lincoln, he said, is “the most famous American who has ever lived.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-7f0000" name="image-7f0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/204b6be/2147483647/strip/true/crop/911x511+0+86/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F2f%2F71%2Fe6c227934206668d06e11b3622b3%2Flincolnhat-cst-04xx12-31-26118407-e1545255011502.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/948b0c5/2147483647/strip/true/crop/911x511+0+86/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F2f%2F71%2Fe6c227934206668d06e11b3622b3%2Flincolnhat-cst-04xx12-31-26118407-e1545255011502.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/14325b6/2147483647/strip/true/crop/911x511+0+86/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F2f%2F71%2Fe6c227934206668d06e11b3622b3%2Flincolnhat-cst-04xx12-31-26118407-e1545255011502.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Figure of Lincoln outside a mock White House at the Abraham Lincoln Presidential Library and Museum in Springfield in 2012. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/14325b6/2147483647/strip/true/crop/911x511+0+86/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F2f%2F71%2Fe6c227934206668d06e11b3622b3%2Flincolnhat-cst-04xx12-31-26118407-e1545255011502.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f711466/2147483647/strip/true/crop/911x511+0+86/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F2f%2F71%2Fe6c227934206668d06e11b3622b3%2Flincolnhat-cst-04xx12-31-26118407-e1545255011502.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/14325b6/2147483647/strip/true/crop/911x511+0+86/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F2f%2F71%2Fe6c227934206668d06e11b3622b3%2Flincolnhat-cst-04xx12-31-26118407-e1545255011502.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Figure of Lincoln outside a mock White House at the Abraham Lincoln Presidential Library and Museum in Springfield in 2012.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Sun-Times file photo</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Friefeld serves on the Lincoln presidential museum board and previously worked as a research historian for the museum, which has an original copy of the Gettysburg Address bearing Lincoln’s signature. He said the museum still houses many rare Lincoln items, but the gloves leaving Lincoln’s hometown is still unfortunate.</p><p>"Of course, it's a loss for the people of Illinois. For a long time, they were at the museum where, every so often, when they went on display, people could see them and have that relationship with history,” Friefeld said. “And of course, it's his blood. What's more Lincoln than his blood, right?"</p>

entries.title: Lincoln's bloody gloves resurface
entries.summary: <h3>It’s Labor Day, Chicago. ✶</h3><p>And that means it's a chance to honor and reflect on the labor of workers nationwide and in our great city.</p><p>It also means summer 2026 is nearing its end — a summer defined by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydauta-l-j/" target="_blank" >deadly heat</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydauta-l-t/" target="_blank" >record-setting storms</a>, a <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydauta-l-i/" target="_blank" >decades-low in murders</a>, swarms of <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydauta-l-d/" target="_blank" >biting bugs</a>, <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydauta-l-h/" target="_blank" >a new addition to the South Side</a> and the excitement of seeing both <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydauta-l-k/" target="_blank" >the Cubs</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydauta-l-u/" target="_blank" >the White Sox</a> inspire playoff dreams.</p><p>But before the beaches and pools officially close, the street festivals wind down and the paleta cart rolls away, we've got a slate of news, good reads and guides to help href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydauta-l-n/" target="_blank" >Sun-Times staff</a></h5><p><b>Workers' parade</b>: Chicagoans celebrated America's labor movements Saturday at the Chicago Labor Day Parade. He made Obama's tan suit.</p><p><b>The pursuit</b>: The Sun-Times' Lynn Sweet has been on the hunt for Obama's tan suit. When he wore it to a press conference on Aug. 28, 2014, right-wing critics deemed it unpresidential. The overblown response to the suit worn by the nation's first Black president sparked a political and cultural flashpoint. It is not at the museum in the Obama Presidential Center in Jackson Park — reporters were told Obama gave the suit away years ago, after cleaning out his closet.</p><p><b>Go deeper</b>: In the latest class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydauta-l-g/" target="_blank" >Tina Sfondeles</a></h5><p><b>New Sox park?</b>: Canal Edge LLC — a company owned by White Sox minority owner Justin Ishbia, who could take over the team as soon as 2034 — is proposing a mixed-use development called The Railyards that he said could be an option presented to the team as its lease at the publicly owned Rate Field ends. The proposal also includes a Northwestern Medicine "health care presence" and "transit-oriented residential, commercial, and retail development."</p><p><b>Railyard rework</b>: The stadium would sit along the Chicago River, stretching from Roosevelt Road to the north to 18th Street to the south, and bordered by the river on its east side and Canal Street to its west. Canal Edge has the land under contract and said the park would turn the Amtrak railyard into a year-round "riverfront venue" with its outfield opening pointed at the city's skyline.</p><p><b>Plan pushback</b>: Ald. Nicole Lee (11th), whose ward encompasses the current Sox stadium in Bridgeport, and Cook County Commissioner John Daley said in a joint statement that "any request for tax breaks and TIF dollars in support of this plan should be roundly rejected." Some cyclists said the ride, absent the car noise and congestion, shows how Chicago’s streets could be designed safer for walkers and cyclists.</p><p>"It's an opportunity to be able to enjoy the full view of Chicago uninterrupted, and it’s always a nice day," said Lakisha Tanner, a returning participant who rides her bike regularly around Chicago.</p><p>The ride is a fundraiser for the Active Transportation Alliance, a non-profit advocating for better conditions for walking, biking and using public transit throughout the Chicago area. About 20,000 participants come out each year.</p><p>Riders had five hours to do the entire 30-mile loop or stick to one section. They could also enter and exit from one of five spots on the route, including the northernmost part at Bryn Mawr Avenue and the southernmost turnaround at 57th Street by the Griffin Museum of Science and Industry. Riders celebrated with coffee, beer and pancakes at a festival in Grant Park.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-ydauta-l-ir/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p>Thanks for reading the Sun-Times! entries.title: Woman charged with fatally shooting another woman in Englewood
entries.summary: <p>A 40-year-old woman has been charged with fatally shooting another woman Friday morning in Englewood, Chicago police said.</p><p>Carlita Jenkins of Englewood is charged with first-degree murder in the death of Candice Latara Michelle Johnson in the 6700 block of South Peoria Avenue. </p><p>Johnson, 37, was walking when Jenkins shot in her chest and back, police said. Johnson was taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center and pronounced dead.</p><p>Police arrested Jenkins three hours later about a quarter mile away in the 900 block of West 68th Street. She was due in court Monday.</p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Man fatally shot in Logan Square, police say
entries.summary: <p>A man was fatally shot Sunday evening near Kosciuszko Park in the Logan Square neighborhood, Chicago police said.</p><p>Officers found the 26-year-old man unresponsive on the ground with a gunshot wound to his back around 8 p.m. in the 2700 block North Harding Avenue, police said in a statement. He was taken to Advocate Illinois Masonic Medical Center and pronounced dead, police said.</p><p>No one has been arrested, police said.</p>

entries.title: 6-month-old dead, 7 others hurt in rollover crash on I-57 in south suburbs
entries.summary: <p>A 6-month-old baby from Chicago was killed in a rollover crash Sunday evening on I-57 in the south suburbs, according to Illinois State Police. </p><p>The infant and seven other people were in a car traveling northbound near 147th Street in Harvey when the vehicle flipped around 5:45 p.m., state police said in a statement. The baby boy, identified as Dakari Lomax of Englewood, was pronounced dead at Ingalls Memorial Hospital, according to state police and the Cook County medical examiner's office.</p><p>The seven other occupants were taken to hospitals with injuries. State police did not report a cause for the crash. No other vehicles were involved.</p><p>Northbound lanes and the 147th Street entrance ramp were closed until around 10:45 p.m. Sunday.</p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Body found in car on Dan Ryan near Rate Field
entries.summary: <p>A dead body was found inside a car Sunday morning on the Dan Ryan Expressway near Rate Field, according to Illinois State Police. </p><p>Troopers discovered the body while responding to a call for the disabled vehicle around 5 a.m. in the southbound lanes of the expressway near 35th Street, state police said in a statement.</p><p>No additional details were shared.</p>

entries.title: EDM-heavy ARC Music Fest brings ‘house home’ with international DJs, local up-and-comers like Virago
entries.summary: <p>ARC Music Festival came booming to life this weekend with the sounds of DJs thundering across the 13 acres of Union Park. LED lights flickered across the park, welcoming fans like Pedro Antonio Navarro, 35, of Pilsen, who quickly made his way to DJ Virago’s stage when gates opened on Friday.</p><p>Virago, whose given name is Sarah Tigges, opened the festival on the main stage with the remixed sounds of William Kiss, Menta Sauce and more.</p><p>“I’m here for the Sarahs,” Navarro quipped, “Virago opens and [Sara] Landry closes.”</p><p>Virago is the type of DJ that ARC has become known for, bridging genres like house and techno with international electronic heavyhitters. For the past five years, Virago has been the musical influence behind the popular local monthly lesbian party “Strapped,” hosted by performers Irregular Girl and Siichele, as well as a monthly night at Splash Nightclub in the Northalsted neighborhood<b>. </b></p><p>She’s also one half of BiPanic, with Valeria Fride, a<b> </b>DJ duo<b> </b>that just made their Lollapalooza premiere this past class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Like many DJs at the ARC Music Festival, Sarah Tigges, aka Virago, stays festival long after her set ends to listen to other performers. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Brittany Sowacke/for WBEZ </p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Her gigs at clubs were long and unforgiving: “Five-hour-long gigs teach you how to work well on the fly,” said Tigges. At first she created complex outlines of her sets with planned transitions and song lists but with time grew confident in her abilities. Now the songs flow from her fingers to your ears, influenced only by how she’s feeling in the moment, nothing else.</p><p>For some, the four day fest is their goodbye to summer, or a welcome break from the slog of an office job. For Tigges, it’s the start of an epic weekend with friends, some of whom flew in just to support her.</p><p>Tigges attended DePaul University to study music business and marketing but quickly realized she was interested in production. She bought her first DJ deck to manipulate music, and after graduating, stayed in Chicago and began producing in earnest.</p><p>Her first gig was at Berlin, the renowned but <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/arts-culture/2026/05/04/decibel-belmont-club-opening-weekend-former-berlin-location-boystown-northalsted" target="_blank" ><u>shuttered nightclub,</u></a> the site of which is now <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/arts-culture/2026/05/04/decibel-belmont-club-opening-weekend-former-berlin-location-boystown-northalsted" target="_blank" ><u>Decibel.</u></a> As a young lesbian, she was happy to be immersed in queer spaces when the rest of nightlife is often predominantly male and straight. “I think we have our finger on the pulse in a different way than a lot of other people do,” she said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-5c0000" she represents a new, younger, generation of DJs who don’t give a f— about appearances or a reel, I think her passion speaks really loudly,” said Tigges’ friend, Jenny Fox, a party promoter and DJ who accompanied Tigges onstage during the set<b>.</b></p><p>“We obviously have great music in NYC, but there’s something special about music in Chicago,” said another friend, Max Palmer, who flew in for Tigges’ set.</p><p>ARC debuted Labor Day weekend in 2021 and was created by John Curley, Stuart Hackley and Nick Karounos, of Auris Presents, the latter formerly associated with the now discontinued fest Spring Awakening. ARC’s tagline is “Where house comes home,” and fittingly, Chicago had a strong influence on this year’s lineup, from stages like The Midway and the Grid to its talent.</p><p>Other ARC performers with local roots included Mike Dunn, an Englewood native and a pioneer of house music; South Side born Honey Dijon; and Lil Louis of “French Kiss” fame.
