entries.title: Armed man charged toward Democratic candidate for Ohio governor at fair, police say
entries.summary: <p>WASHINGTON — An armed assailant charged toward the Democratic candidate for Ohio governor, Amy Acton, on Sunday during a campaign stop at the Canfield Fair, injuring several people before he was stopped by troopers, the Ohio State Highway Patrol said.</p><p>The Ohio State Highway Patrol said in a statement that a man it identified as Patrick Havas, 38, forced his way through a crowd, knocking over multiple members of the audience as he moved toward Acton, the state's former public health director. He had a taser and two pistols, the statement said.</p><p>The Mahoning County Sheriff’s Office said two handguns and a set of brass knuckles were recovered after his arrest, and “no weapons were ever brandished or even removed from their holsters.”</p><p>Havas was taken to the county jail and booked on charges of disorderly conduct and two counts of assault, the highway patrol statement said, adding that no other details were available pending an investigation. Online court records didn’t yet list the case, and it wasn’t clear as of Sunday night whether Havas has an attorney.</p><p>Republican Gov. Mike DeWine said in a statement that the man “tried to forcefully push himself” toward Acton as she was speaking at the fair in Canfield, in northeastern Ohio. “Violence or the threat of violence at political or public events is always unacceptable," he added.</p><p>The attempted attack is the latest political violence to roil the United States. And the Ohio gubernatorial race is one of the most high-profile races this year as the campaigns enter the final six weeks of campaigning before the election in November.</p><p>Acton is facing Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, who has parlayed his national name recognition, tech industry connections and alliance with President Donald Trump into a record fundraising haul that he is tapping for advertising spots aimed at the November election. He is using campaign rallies and advertising to criticize Acton.</p><p>Ramaswamy's campaign called the incident Sunday unacceptable.</p><p>“Candidates should be able to meet with voters without having to worry about threats or violence. What happened today is completely unacceptable and has no place in politics, and we hope hope that no one was hurt,” Ramaswamy’s communications director, Connie Luck, said in a statement.</p><p>Addie Bullock, communications director for Acton's campaign, said in a statement that the suspect “lunged” at Acton. She said the Democratic candidate “will always stand up to the chaos, hate and vitriol that pits us against one another.”</p><p>The incident brought condemnation from Ohio Republican Sen. Jon Husted, who said on X that he and his wife were “disturbed by the attempted attack on Amy Acton today at the Canfield Fair. We are grateful for law enforcement’s quick response. There is no place for this kind of behavior, and it must never be tolerated.”</p><p>The country has seen a rise in political violence over the past decade. That includes the 2017 shooting at a Republican congressional baseball team practice in Alexandria, Virginia; the 2022 hammer assault on the husband of Democratic then-House Speaker Nancy Pelosi in California; the 2024 assassination attempt on Donald Trump at a Pennsylvania rally during his presidential campaign as well as another on the president at this year's White House Correspondents' Association Dinner in April; and the assassinations last year of a Democratic Minnesota state lawmaker and her husband and of conservative commentator Charlie Kirk in Utah.</p><p>Federal political committees spent more than $40 million on expenses labeled as security during the 2023-24 campaign cycle, the most recent one for which data is publicly available, according a report released in April from the Public Service Alliance, a nonpartisan group that focuses on security for public officials.</p><p>Before running for governor, Acton was recruited by DeWine in 2019 to lead the Ohio Department of Health while serving as an associate professor of public health at Ohio State University. As the COVID-19 pandemic ramped up in early 2020, she was thrown into the state and national spotlight — becoming a source of comfort to many viewers of the governor’s daily news conferences.</p><p>For her service as health director, Acton earned the John F. Kennedy Library Foundation’s Profile in COVID Courage Award, the Columbus Foundation’s Spirit of Columbus Award and Ohio State’s highest alumni honor, the Alumni Medalist Award.</p><p>Her position as the face of the DeWine administration’s aggressive stance against the virus also earned Acton many enemies, among them Statehouse Republicans and average Ohioans who opposed pandemic restrictions.</p>

entries.title: Fuel prices at record Labor Day high in US thanks to Iran War and refinery issues
entries.summary: <p>It's never been more expensive in the U.S. to fill up the tank and take one last summer trip over the Labor Day weekend.</p><p>The average price of regular gas was $4.14 a gallon heading into the holiday, nearly a dollar higher than last year and well above the Labor Day weekend record of $3.82 from 2012, according to AAA motor club.</p><p>Nicole Collins planned to head from Philadelphia to South Carolina to visit friends, but she said her family has spent most of the summer close to home and not taking their typical weekend trips because driving has gotten so expensive.</p><p>“Gas is pretty high right now. It doesn’t help that we also have a baby, so we also have to pay for that,” Collins said outside a gas station in Claymont, Delaware, where regular gas was $4.199 a gallon.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/transportation/2026/09/03/labor-day-weekend-travel" target="_blank" >Here’s what to expect while traveling over Labor Day weekend</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Prices shot up after the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in February and have not settled down since. Crude oil traffic through the key Strait of Hormuz has plunged, and Iran has refused to reopen the waterway.</p><p>“Everything points to the Iran War and the Strait of Hormuz,” said Tom Seng, a professor of energy finance at Texas Christian University.</p><p>Energy Secretary Chris Wright offered few specifics on when the nation’s drivers might see relief at the gas pump, acknowledging that prices are higher now than Labor Day 2025.</p><p>“Yes, they’re higher today, but we’re doing everything we can to push them down," Wright said Sunday on ABC’s “This Week.”</p><p>The national average for regular gas prices is still well below the record of $5.02 a gallon set in June 2022.</p><p>But diesel is a different story: It hit a national average of $5.85 a gallon Friday, a record.</p><p>Trucks and other freight delivery systems use a lot of diesel, and that increased transportation cost is being passed on to consumers, whether at the grocery store or through package delivery services.</p><p>“It doesn’t really seem like there’s an end to it,” Collins said.</p><p>Gas prices typically drop as the summer driving season ends and refineries turn to making a cheaper winter blend.</p><p>But Seng said there are other factors this year even beyond the volatile situation in the Middle East that make future prices unpredictable. U.S. refineries are working at 98% capacity, many in the unusually harsh Texas heat. If there are problems there or a hurricane knocks some systems offline, prices will struggle to drop.</p><p>And it's not just a Middle East problem. Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian refineries are squeezing diesel supplies. Chinese refiners are seeing declining outputs as well, said Matthew Metzgar, a clinical professor of economics at UNC Charlotte.</p><p>“There’s just less gasoline coming out of those refineries,” Metzgar said.</p><p>Wright, the energy secretary, said the Trump administration was taking steps to increase production and that the markets forecast lower prices in the coming months.</p><p>“If you look at the futures prices, if you wanted to buy today in bulk gasoline for two months out in November, it’s about $0.35 cheaper than it is today. So the marketplace thinks gasoline prices are going to move meaningfully lower," he said.</p><p>Geopolitically, though, there is little a driver can do to knock down gas prices.</p><p>But using price apps can help save a little money, especially on long trips where gas by the interstate could be 10 to 15 cents per gallon more expensive than at stations a short drive down the road, Metzgar said.</p>

entries.title: Federal investigators probe Amazon cargo jet's runway crash that killed 5 in Miami
entries.summary: <p>MIAMI — Federal investigators examining why an Amazon cargo jet barreled off a runway at Miami International Airport and into vehicles, killing at least five people, are likely to focus on a crucial moment in the landing: whether the plane touched down too late to stop safely.</p><p>Video of Sunday’s landing appears to show the Boeing 767 remaining airborne well down the runway before touching down. Aviation experts said investigators will seek to determine exactly where the plane landed and, if it was beyond the normal touchdown zone, why the pilots did not abandon the landing and circle back for another attempt.</p><p>Investigators will also examine the plane’s speed and braking, weather and wind conditions, the aircraft’s mechanical condition and other factors that could have contributed to the deadly overrun. The National Transportation Safety Board has sent a team led by Chairwoman Jennifer Homendy to Miami, where she is expected to give the agency’s first briefing on the investigation Monday.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/nation-world/2026/09/06/amazon-cargo-plane-crash-miami" target="_blank" >At least 5 dead after Amazon cargo plane barrels off runway at Miami airport</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>The aircraft overran the runway around 2 p.m. Sunday after arriving from San Juan, Puerto Rico, and plowed across a road used by warehouse workers and other businesses that surround the airport. Five people died, three were critically injured and two others were hospitalized with less severe injuries, officials said.</p><p>The crash, which sent thick black smoke billowing into the sky, trapped the pilot and copilot in the cockpit and some occupants in cars, said Miami-Dade Fire Rescue Chief Ray Jadallah. The agency said crews also had to extricate a person who was trapped under a vehicle. It wasn’t immediately clear if the pilots were among those killed.</p><p>The typical landing zone for a plane is within the first 3,000 feet of a runway, experts said. If the cargo jet was beyond that area, it should have aborted the landing and gone around for another try, aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said.</p><p>Mary Schiavo, who is a pilot and former Inspector General of the Transportation Department, said video posted online shows the Amazon plane floating above the runway for an extended period without flaring the nose upward to force the main landing gear onto the ground.</p><p>It wasn’t raining at the time, but dark storm clouds loomed and strong winds were reported. Schiavo said that if the plane had a tail wind, that could have contributed to it floating further down the runway.</p><p>“A tail wind would certainly add to your troubles if you’ve already given up a good chunk of the runway by not touching down and landing right away,” Schiavo said.</p><p>The Miami airport is not equipped with arresting systems that the FAA says have been installed at more than 120 airports nationwide to safely stop planes that do go past the end of a runway. Those beds of lightweight, crushable material at the end of a runway have been credited by the FAA with helping save at least 497 lives aboard planes that overran runways.</p><p>The crash halted flights at the busy travel hub for much of the afternoon. Some 200 emergency personnel responded, finding the plane with heavy flames and smoke from a complex engine compartment fire, the department said. Firefighters used foam from specialized airport firefighting units to extinguish the fire, and crews were still dealing with a fuel leak on the plane hours later.</p><p>The Prime Air plane came to rest beside a roadway near two semitrucks, images showed. The aircraft appeared to be resting on its belly and was largely intact despite the fire.</p><p>The flight had been operated by 21 Air, a cargo carrier based in North Carolina. The 32-year-old Boeing 767 was originally built to carry passengers and flew for several airlines for more than two decades before being converted to a cargo plane in 2015, according to flight-tracking site Flightradar24.</p><p>Schiavo said the NTSB will also closely examine the maintenance history of this plane — particularly since it has a history of foreign ownership, including by a Russian company.</p><p>Last year, a UPS plane crashed after losing its engine while accelerating down the runway at Louisville’s Muhammad Ali International Airport. The crash killed all three pilots and 12 people on the ground. Twenty-three more were injured.</p>

entries.title: 6 killed, 17 hurt in Labor Day weekend gun violence
entries.summary: <p>Nearly two dozen people have been shot in Chicago so far over the Labor Day holiday weekend.</p><p>Of the 23 people shot since 5 p.m. Friday, six have died from their injuries, according to Chicago police. Two teenagers were wounded in separate shootings.</p><p>As of Monday morning, the weekend's violence was lower than <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2025/09/02/labor-day-weekend-violence-crime-brandon-johnson-donald-trump" target="_blank" >last Labor Day weekend</a>, when nine people were killed and 52 wounded.</p><p>Labor Day marks the end of summer. And this season has been historically peaceful in Chicago, compared to past years.</p><p>The city had 122 murders in June, July and August — the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/09/02/chicago-violence-mayor-johnson-giannoulias-quigley-mendoza" target="_blank" >lowest summer total since 1965</a>. Last year, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/01/01/chicago-crime-murder-homicide-shooting-president-trump-mayor-johnson" target="_blank" >total violence also hit record lows</a> for the first time in decades.</p><p>Despite decreasing violence, six people have been killed and 18 wounded this weekend in shootings mainly on the South and West sides. One person was also injured in a stabbing Friday night.</p><p>The first fatal shooting happened during an argument <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/09/05/man-fatally-shot-after-argument-in-chicago-lawn" target="_blank" >Friday night in Chicago Lawn</a>. Josh Washington, 28, was fatally shot in his abdomen by a person he was arguing with in the 7300 block of South Kedzie Avenue.</p><p>At around 2 a.m. Saturday, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/09/05/man-fatally-shot-by-2-people-in-west-englewood" target="_blank" >two people fatally shot a man</a> in West Englewood. Enderson Linares, 29, was in the 6500 block of South Laflin Street when the two people shot him and fled in a blue sedan. Linares, who lived on the block where he was killed, was pronounced dead at the scene.</p><p>A woman was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/09/06/woman-fatally-shot-near-west-side-home" target="_blank" >found in a Near West Side home</a> suffering from several gunshot wounds just after midnight Sunday. Officers discovered the woman, who has not been identified, inside the home in the 2100 block of West Jackson Boulevard. She was pronounced dead at Stroger Hospital. </p><p>A <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/09/06/austin-shooting-jerome-kirk" target="_blank" >Springfield man was fatally shot</a> Sunday afternoon in the Austin neighborhood. Jerome Kirk, 20, was sitting in a car in the 300 block of North Lamon Avenue when a person walked up to the vehicle and fired shots.</p><p>A 26-year-old man was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/09/07/logan-square-shooting" target="_blank" >fatally shot Sunday evening</a> near Kosciuszko Park in the Logan Square neighborhood. Officers found the man, who has not been identified, unresponsive on the ground with a gunshot wound to his back in the 2700 block North Harding Avenue.</p><p>Around 7:30 a.m. Monday, a 27-year-old woman was found fatally shot in her head inside a Woodlawn home in the 6300 block of South Vernon Avenue. She was pronounced dead at the scene. Police said they were conducting a homicide investigation.</p><p>This summer's two other holiday weekends also saw below-average levels of violence. </p><p>Memorial Day was the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/05/24/17-people-shot-overnight-chicago" target="_blank" >least deadly weekend</a> for the holiday in 16 years. Two people died and at least 38 were wounded in Chicago.</p><p>Five people were killed and 23 were hurt in the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/07/06/july-fourth-weekend-violence-total-homicides-shootings-injured" target="_blank" >least violent Fourth of July weekend</a> in at least seven years. </p>

entries.title: The Bears won the Panthers trade — and now need to win because of it
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> won their <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2023/3/10/23625134/bears-trade-no-1-pick-nfl-draft-panthers-justin-fields-ryan-poles-bryce-young-will-anderson-nfl-deal" target="_blank" >2023 trade</a> with the Panthers.</p><p></p><p>The only question remaining is by how wide a margin — and whether they can parlay that windfall into consistent success. Winning a trade, after all, means nothing unless you win a championship.</p><p></p><p>That will be decided by quarterback <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/09/03/bears-caleb-williams-hot-ones-debut-top-5-moments-ben-johnson-quarterback-nfl-hot-wings" target="_blank" >Caleb Williams</a>, whom the Bears need to make another leap in Year 3 before they commit to giving him the largest contract extension in team history. If he does, then general manager Ryan Poles’ decision to flip the franchise’s first modern-era No.1 pick for receiver DJ Moore and four draft picks could go down as the most impactful trade in franchise history.</p><p></p><p>Even if Williams never reaches that point, there’s no question the deal pointed the Bears in the right direction. Bryce Young, the quarterback the Panthers took with the first pick, is 14-30 in his first three seasons. He’s eligible now for the same contract extension Williams may get next offseason — and the Panthers have made zero effort to secure a deal before the Panthers host the Bears in Sunday’s season opener.</p><p></p><p>By contrast, Bears’ return in the trade — and the small trades they spun off of it — is the foundation of a roster that won the NFC North last year:</p><p></p><p>• Williams, the first pick in 2024, has already won more playoff games than the last major Bears trade acquisition, Khalil Mack, ever did. After a year in which he led the NFL in fourth-quarter comebacks Bears want him to improve his completion percentage and get off to faster starts.</p><p></p><p>• Darnell Wright, whom the Bears drafted 10<sup>th</sup> overall in 2023 — after trading back from the Panthers’ original No. 9 spot so the Eagles could take star Jalen Carter — just</p><p>earned the largest contract extension ever for a right tackle.</p><p></p><p>• Moore averaged 1,008 receiving yards in three seasons with the Bears before being traded to the Bills for a second-round pick, which the Bears traded down from, eventually picking tight end Sam Roush in Round 3.</p><p></p><p>• Luther Burden, whom the Bears drafted in Round 2 last year, was dynamic enough that the Bears could afford to trade Moore.</p><p></p><p>• Cornerback Tyrique Stevenson has been a starter — though an inconsistent one — for three years.</p><p></p><p>• Punter Tory Taylor is entering his third season with the Bears.</p><p></p><p>The Panthers were the first team to approach Poles about a trade in February 2023. He chose their offer after trying to keep them at bay for weeks. While negotiating with Carolina, he tried to loop in the Texans, who were picking second and would eventually take C.J. Stroud. Poles was trying to trade down to No. 2, and then flip that pick to the Panthers. Eventually, the Texans disengaged.</p><p></p><p>There are times when Poles lays in bed and wonders where the Bears would be had he not swung the trade. In the moment, though, he wasn't positive the deal would work. There were too many unknowns — from which quarterback the Panthers would take to where they’d finish the following year when the Bears held their draft selection — to make a clean evaluation.</p><p></p><p>It took nerve. He was the general manager of the Bears, who are synonymous with quarterback failure, declining to draft a quarterback first overall — and choosing to give Justin Fields another year. Fields proved he wasn't the answer. Had the Panthers not finished with the worst record in the NFL in 2024, the whole gambit might not have worked.</p><p></p><p>“You don’t want to be the person that misses on the quarterback, and there’s no guarantee where you’re going to be the following year,” Poles said. “Just the pressure of putting everything together, from your gut instinct to the data to projections. … All of this is really high-end educated guesses. You don’t know. But you just have to put all the information that you do know together to make the best decision.”</p><p></p><p>What he did know, though, was that the Bears needed a talent infusion before selfish established in the Bears’ 3-14 season took root permanently. That’s why Poles insisted on an established veteran — the two sides settled on Moore — being included in the deal.</p><p></p><p>“You’re in this rush of really trying to have some success because the guys that are fighting every year, … their career is going only so long, and you need some positive outcomes to keep everyone’s heads up,” he said. “There is a side effect of being bad for a long time. Usually it’s, everyone just focuses on their own career rather than the team.”</p><p></p><p>That’s what happened in Carolina — and, eventually, at Halas Hall.</p><p></p><p>The Panthers fired head coach Frank Reich after going 1-10 through the first 11 games of Young’s rookie year. Young lost his starting job in 2024 and didn’t get it back until Andy Dalton, his replacement, injured his thumb in a car accident.</p><p></p><p>During Williams’ rookie year, the Bears fired offensive coordinator and then, after a 4-8 start, head coach Matt Eberflus. Ben Johnson picked the Bears — and vice versa — in part because the team had Williams.</p><p></p><p>“How we’re constructed, obviously, it was a huge deal for when we go to the head coaching search,” Poles said. “Obviously, Ben being the top candidate around the league. You want to be in position to have a guy like that be interested and want to come on board and put his fingerprints on the team.”</p>

entries.title: Authorities identify woman found fatally shot in Near West Side home
entries.summary: <p>A 42-year-old woman was found fatally shot inside a Near West Side home early Sunday, Chicago police said.</p><p>Officers discovered her inside the home in the 2100 block of West Jackson Boulevard around 12:05 a.m., police said. She was shot several times and was taken to Stroger Hospital where she was pronounced dead, according to police.</p><p>The Cook County medical examiner's office identified her Monday as Crystal Salter.</p><p>No one has been arrested, police said.</p><p><i>Editor's note: This story has been updated to correct the day of the shooting to Sunday.</i></p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Bears practice report: RB Kyle Monangai returns
entries.summary: <p>Breaking down the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a>’ Monday practice:</p><h3><b>Monangai back, Odunze still out</b></h3><p>Three weeks and one day after he hurt his knee when he got tangled with defensive tackle Grady Jarrett during an unpadded drill, running back Kyle Monangai returned to practice. He worked during the Bears’ brief 40-minute practice at Halas Hall. Monangai had 783 rushing yards on 169 carries as a rookie.</p><p>Running back D’Andre Swift, who left practice Thursday with a cramp, practiced. So did every single Bears player but receiver Rome Odunze, who left practice Thursday after appearing to injure the same right foot that hampered him last year. A source said last week that preliminary indications were that the injury wasn’t considered serious. Odunze, who described keeping tabs on his foot his “new normal” hadn’t missed a significant snap all training camp until Thursday.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/09/04/bears-colston-loveland-taylor-swift-travis-kelce-wedding-tight-end-rare-diamond-ben-johnson-cole-kmet-nfl-training-camp" target="_blank" >Bears</a> don’t have to submit an injury report until Wednesday.</p><h3>Game week</h3><p>It didn’t rookie hit Dillon Thieneman until he got the weekend off — he was about to play his first NFL game. The first-round safety had spent most of training camp trying to get through practice — and then the three-game preseason schedule.</p><p>“[Sunday] night I was watching film, prepping for the game,” he said. “It’s kind of like, ‘Geez, I’m really where I wanted to be being that little kid.’”</p><h3><b>What’s next</b></h3><p>The Bears will practice Tuesday at Halas Hall as they continue preparations for the season opener against the Panthers.</p>
entries.author: Patrick Finley

entries.title: Man, 45, critically wounded in South Shore shooting
entries.summary: <p>A 45-year-old man was shot and critically injured by a man on a scooter in South Shore on Monday afternoon, Chicago police said.</p><p>The victim had been standing near the sidewalk along the 7800 block of South South Shore Drive at about 2:53 p.m. when the other man approached him on a scooter and fired multiple shots at him, police said. </p><p>The 45-year-old man suffered multiple gunshot wounds to his body and was taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center, police said.</p><p>The victim was initially listed in critical condition, according to police. </p><p>Area Two detectives are investigating. Police said two persons of interest were brought in for questioning.</p>

entries.title: Cubs laud Brewers as among baseball's best, but shouldn't Cubs be, too? It doesn't look like it
entries.summary: <p>MILWAUKEE — Cubs manager Craig Counsell made an interesting remark after a 4-3 loss to the Brewers on Monday that dropped his team a season-high eight games back of the National League Central leaders.</p><p>“When you play the best teams in the league, you have to do a lot of things right to beat them,” he said. “We did a lot of things right, but you have to do almost everything right to beat them.”</p><p>He was referring to the Brewers, of course, but shouldn’t he be referring to the Cubs, as well?</p><p>After all, the Cubs have some of the deepest pockets in baseball, they’re thought to have won the trade deadline and they have the best player in the game in Pete Crow-Armstrong. Aren’t they one of the best teams in the league?</p><p>The standings say so. The Cubs have the fifth-best winning percentage in the NL, but that’s only good enough for a wild-card spot as a road team. And would any potential playoff opponent be scared to face them in the best-of-three round?</p><p>These are the 2026 Cubs: good enough to compete, not good enough to win.</p><p>Another second-place finish awaits them after the Brewers did what the Brewers do, outscoring their opponent without hitting a home run — the Cubs outhomered them 2-0 — and delivering timely hits that drive the opposition nuts.</p><p>After the Cubs took the lead in the fifth inning on Pedro Ramirez’s homer, the Brewers answered in the bottom half on a single, a sacrifice bunt and Garrett Mitchell’s RBI single.</p><p>After the Cubs took the lead in the seventh with Brewers-like hitting — a single, a walk and Alex Bregman’s RBI single, all with two outs — the Brewers responded with three runs in the eighth, the big blow being Jackson Chourio’s go-ahead, two-run single.</p><p>Crow-Armstrong added to his legend with two stolen bases, giving him 35, and a homer in the ninth, giving him 41. But two outstanding defensive plays in that inning sealed the Cubs’ fate. Right fielder Luis Lara leaped at the wall to rob Ramirez of extra bases right before Crow-Armstrong’s blast, and left fielder Chourio stole a hit from Seiya Suzuki with a sliding grab.</p><p>Aren’t the Cubs the best defensive team in baseball? The Brewers can beat them there, too?</p><p>Even an outstanding performance from starter Matthew Boyd wasn’t enough. He pitched into the eighth, allowing three runs. But the bullpen gave up the fourth, which was the difference. And like Counsell said, against the best teams in the league, the margins are paper-thin.</p><p>“That’s what it comes down to with good baseball and baseball that you play at the end of the year with good teams,” said Boyd, who set the table for the Brewers’ eighth by walking Mitchell and allowing a double to Joey Ortiz. “This speaks to their ability.</p><p>“It’s something that I believe is a big part of our game, winning in those margins. And that’s something that they’ve done, that’s led them to those division titles over the past few years. They don’t give you much, and that’s what makes them so good.”</p><p>But aren’t the Cubs supposed to be so good? They’re on track to finish second to the Brewers for the third consecutive season under Counsell, whom the Cubs stole from the Brewers to beat them at their own game. The Brewers also clinched the season series and own the tiebreaker.</p><p>What happens if the Cubs make the wild-card round but lose, or they advance but lose to the Brewers in the NL Division Series for the second straight year? Counsell will enter the penultimate year of his contract next season. Team president Jed Hoyer received an extension last year. How many second-place finishes do they get?</p><p>With 17 games left and one of the toughest remaining schedules in baseball, the Cubs could have more at stake than just a playoff spot.</p><bsp-listcarousel class="PageListE" data-module data-column-count=3 data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-hide-descriptions="true" entries.title: Cubs reliever Ryan Rolison heeds advice from wife, who said he was 'boring to watch'
entries.summary: <p>MILWAUKEE — If you’ve enjoyed watching the emotion Cubs left-handed reliever Ryan Rolison has shown lately, you can thank his wife, Lauren. When Rolison came home from work one night, she shared a brutally honest opinion of her husband’s pitching.</p><p>“You’re kind of boring to watch,” she said.</p><p>“That was a wake-up call for me to flip the switch and get back to what I’m capable of,” Rolison told the Sun-Times on Monday. “Talking to her and some of the pitching coaches, we’re emptying the tank now. It’s playoff-push time. I’m thinking you’re going to see a lot more fire.</p><p>“I think that I pitch better when I have a little edge to me, a little fire. I was sick of the way I was throwing the ball.”</p><p>But there’s more to Rolison’s recent success than letting his emotions out. Though he’s putting up good numbers overall, Rolison said he had been frustrated with his performance since the All-Star break, particularly against right-handed hitters.</p><p>“[They] were killing me on some pitches,” he said. “With them, I feel like I got too predictable. So we went back and broke down some of the numbers of what my sequences are for them, mixing in some other pitches. We’ve seen progress with that the past few outings.”</p><p>Those include earning a save against the Brewers last week with a perfect ninth inning in which Rolison induced a weak groundout from righty Andrew Vaughn. He also earned a win — his eighth — against the Marlins over the weekend, striking out righty pinch hitter Agustin Ramirez, though he did allow a double to Esteury Ruiz, another righty pinch hitter.</p><p>“I’ve been pretty good all year against lefties, but if I can limit slug against the right-handed hitters to get to a lefty …,” said Rolison, who figures to get more looks in high-leverage spots. “Throwing the ball with confidence, trusting my stuff in the zone, has been the biggest thing. Not trying to be perfect out there and just being very aggressive in the zone.”</p><p>Rolison said he’s a different pitcher this year than he was as a rookie last year with the Rockies, and the numbers show that. This year, he has a 2.89 ERA in 56 innings. Last year, he had a 7.02 ERA in 42 ⅓ innings.</p><p>“It kind of looks like two different pitchers, from confidence to arsenal, from velocity,” Rolison said. “I’ve thrown my sinker a lot in the second half, and it’s been really successful against left-handed hitters. I think that you’re going to see a lot more sinkers to righties.”</p><p>And a lot more emotion to everyone.</p><h3>Swanson nearing ramp-up</h3><p>Shortstop Dansby Swanson continues to progress in his recovery from a strained left oblique.</p><p>“Everything is good with Dansby,” manager Craig Counsell said. “We are probably getting closer to hopefully putting a final schedule together. I think he will progress to the higher-velocity hitting as we get home this weekend. Then I think we’re ready to start talking about playing in games.”</p><p>Swanson left the game Aug. 16 with the injury. If he were to return next week on the homestand, he’d miss almost exactly a month, at the low end of the time he was projected to miss.</p><h3>Notes</h3><p>The Cubs’ trip from Miami was affected by the crash of an Amazon cargo plane that overran a runway and killed five people, forcing a ground stop. Their charter was diverted to Fort Lauderdale, and travel director Vijay Tekchandani worked some magic to get everyone’s luggage moved from Miami.</p><p>• Left fielder Ian Happ returned to action Monday after being scratched Sunday because of a bruised knee. He pinch-hit for Tyrone Taylor in the sixth and stayed in the game. Happ didn’t start because the Brewers started a left-hander, Robert Gasser.</p><p>• Right-hander Shelby Miller pitched in back-to-back games for the first time in his recovery from Tommy John surgery, combining for one inning Friday and Saturday at Triple-A Iowa. Counsell said Miller came out of it feeling good.</p><bsp-listcarousel class="PageListE" data-module data-column-count=3 data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" entries.title: CFD: 1 dead on CTA Red Line tracks near 63rd Street
entries.summary: <p>Chicago Fire Department personnel found a person dead on the Chicago Transit Authority Red Line tracks near 69th Street on the South Side Monday afternoon, officials said.</p><p>A spokesman said an individual was found dead when they responded to a call of a person on the tracks at around 2:36 p.m. </p><p>CFD could not immediately provide additional information about the circumstances of the incident.</p><p>The CTA issued an alert at 3:35 p.m. notifying riders that Red Line trains were running with major delays after a medical emergency on the tracks near 69th Street.</p><p>Bus shuttles were made available from 43rd to 95th streets in both directions to supplement service in the affected areas through 4 p.m., a CTA alert said.</p>

entries.title: White Sox nearing surprising AL Central title behind remodeled player acquisition process
entries.summary: <p>As White Sox general manager Chris Getz introduced the acquisition of Luis Castillo to reporters last month, he didn’t reference the last-minute looks teams notoriously send professional scouts for before the trade deadline.</p><p>Rather, he mentioned the boost to his team’s fortunes foretold by their internal projection systems, the “stuff grades” indicating the 33-year-old still had the weapons to get outs despite career-worst results. It’s a different language than what previous occupants of his role used.</p><p>“It starts with the projection system,” Getz told the Sun-Times about the team’s remodeled process for acquiring players. “Then it’s ‘how does that connect with our pro scouting group?’ Or whoever is evaluating from a scouting lens, and then biomechanically, what does the engine look like?”</p><p>With a 7.52 ERA in a Sox uniform, Castillo–like all four White Sox major-league acquisitions at the deadline–has not instantly installed team-prescribed tweaks and hit the ground running. But if you don’t love these new White Sox for shipping out prospects for two-time Gold Glove-winner Brenton Doyle to post a .537 OPS in his first month with the team, you don’t deserve them being four games up in the loss column on second-place Cleveland with 19 left to play, thank to a lineup powered unheralded acquisitions turned into player development breakthroughs like Miguel Vargas and Tristan Peters.</p><p>Next year, when the White Sox could be coming off the seventh, and possibly most surprising division title in franchise history, they’ll need more immediate impact than the sort of fixer-uppers that can be acquired midseason without costing prospects Caleb Bonemer and Billy Carlson in exchange. But if Castillo and Doyle look sharper later in their White Sox tenure, with adjustments and opportunity, it would very much fit their growing brand.</p><p>“We've had enough success stories that why would we reroute from that approach?” Getz said. “There could be perhaps an adjustment in that thought process at some point in the future where it's not about runway, we need production you know right out of the gate.”</p><p>But that would be a good problem, and an earned one.</p><p>This is the second season the White Sox have operated with a “department of acquisition,” led by Matt Grabowski, who like assistant general manager Josh Barfield, was hired away from Diamondbacks player development after their 2023 National League title. Where pro scouting, international scouting, player development, biomechanists, training staff, etc., once struggled to align in the Sox org, if they were properly supported at all, the acquisitions departments is a means of getting everyone on the same page with a game plan for any new addition.</p><p>“We've gotten to a place where everybody's comfortable understanding what role they play in player acquisition,” Barfield said during the team’s road series in Houston. “[The acquisition department] is kind of a hub, and you have the spokes off that.”</p><p>The spokes include the bat-speed training used to vault Vargas, Peters and Chase Meidroth from judicious, contact-oriented swingers into the most valuable players in their division at their respective positions. Or the pitching instruction that turned hard-throwing Jordan Hicks from a salary dump acquisition from Boston, to someone striking out 37% of hitters since a June arm angle adjustment. Sox statistical analysts who fetishize unique release angles have brought in numerous funky-looking relievers over the last two years, but struck gold with Bryan Hudson, whose long limbs and low arm slot have made his 92 mph heater one of the best pitches in the sport.</p><p>Even the signature signing of slugger Munetaka Murakami from Japan is representative of the White Sox both using the ample opportunity their developing roster could offer unproven players, and recognizing East Asian pro leagues as an avenue for finding undervalued players like Anthony Kay, who fit their modest payroll.</p><p>“The checklist remains still pretty simple: it's body, athlete, tools, makeup,” special assistant David Keller, who heads the team’s international operations. “Then taking the player through [researching and development] scrubbing, where we look heavily into the data and the analytics, whatever we have access to, getting their take, taking all of that information, presenting it to to our respective heads of departments, whether it's [pitching] Brian Bannister or [hitting] Ryan Fuller.”</p><p>The amateur baseball world is where the operation works in reverse, with scouts suggesting players for statistical review. But Getz insists there is still a role for in-person pro scouting to identify factors their projection system cannot yet capture. One easy example to point to is makeup. Why have these young Sox only had one four-game losing streak? Maybe, they’re willing to suggest, because they’re tough.</p><p>“We're very cautious with what we bring in,” Barfield said. “[Makeup] is something that we value, maybe more than other teams.”</p><p>Making the leap from a 100-plus losses to seven-games over .500 is hard, but becoming a perennial contender is even harder. Barfield and Getz both brought up the case of Curtis Mead, another buy-low acquisition who couldn’t put it together before the Sox shipped him out and watched him bloom elsewhere, as evidence that opportunities to give players runway to develop will shrink as their yearly expectations heighten.</p><p>With more pressure, the work of balancing these different departments and potential factions within the organization should grow harder. But that’s where the Sox actually don’t see trouble on the horizon.</p><p>“It begins and ends with Chris,” Keller said of baseball operations’ cohesion. “The ultimate goal is to win, and the understanding and the emphasis is that we're going to work together to do this.”</p>
entries.author: James Fegan
